topic: Digital signals, codes and spread spectrum

notes.front: How does quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) carry data?
notes.back: By modulating the amplitude of two carriers of the same frequency that are 90 degrees out of phase.
notes.explanation: The two carriers are in quadrature, so each can be modulated separately on the same frequency.
notes.example: Like two sine waves a quarter-cycle apart, each turned up and down by its own share of the data.
notes.evidence: B. Transmission of data by modulating the amplitude of two carriers of the same frequency but 90 degrees out of phase

notes.front: On a constellation diagram of a QAM or QPSK signal, what does each point represent?
notes.back: One possible phase-and-amplitude state for a symbol.
notes.explanation: The diagram maps every state a symbol can take, so it shows the signal's alphabet rather than its frequency response.
notes.example: Like a map of marked parking bays: every symbol must stop in one of them.
notes.evidence: What is described by the constellation diagram of a QAM or QPSK signal? A. How many carriers may be present at the same time B. The possible phase and amplitude states for each symbol

notes.front: Under Part 97, what is a transmission's necessary bandwidth?
notes.back: The bandwidth needed for its information rate and emission type; good amateur practice says occupy no more.
notes.explanation: Emissions from modulation must also stay within the band or segment the control operator may use.
notes.example: Like a lorry keeping to its own lane, and the lane only as wide as the load needs.
notes.evidence: (a) No amateur station transmission shall occupy more bandwidth than necessary for the information rate and emission type being transmitted, in accordance with good amateur practice. (b) Emissions resulting from modulation must be confined to the band or segment available to the control operator.

notes.front: How is rise time defined?
notes.back: The time for the voltage to build up from 10 to 90 per cent of its maximum amplitude.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two transient intervals of a pulse; fall time is the other, on the way down.
notes.example: Like timing a car from 10 to 90 per cent of its top speed, ignoring the slow start and finish.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 9, chapter 3, pulse transient intervals, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: The two types of transient intervals are RISE TIME and FALL TIME. Rise time is more accurately defined as the time required for the voltage to build up from 10 percent to 90 percent of the maximum amplitude point.

notes.front: What are key clicks?
notes.back: Interference heard as clicks or thumps, caused by the sudden application and removal of power when keying CW.
notes.explanation: The rapid current surges can disturb receivers tuned well away from the transmitter's frequency.
notes.example: Like the pop from a loudspeaker switched on abruptly, but radiated across the band.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 1, key clicks, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: However, the sudden application and removal of power causes rapid surges of current which may cause interference in nearby receivers. Even though such receivers are tuned to frequencies far removed from that of the transmitter, interference may be present in the form of "clicks" or "thumps."

notes.front: What is special about Gray code?
notes.back: Only one bit changes between sequential code values.
notes.explanation: In plain binary counting several bits can flip at once, as from 0111 to 1000; Gray code avoids that.
notes.example: Like a counter where only one wheel is ever allowed to turn at each step.
notes.evidence: E8C09 (D) Which digital code allows only one bit to change between sequential code values? A. Binary Coded Decimal Code B. Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code C. Extended ASCII D. Gray code

notes.front: What is ASCII, as Part 97 describes it?
notes.back: The 7-unit International Alphabet No. 5 code, one of the digital codes Part 97 names.
notes.explanation: Part 97 lists it beside the 5-unit Baudot code as a code amateurs may use for RTTY and data emissions.
notes.example: Like a table giving each letter, number and symbol its own 7-bit pattern.
notes.evidence: (3) The 7-unit, International Alphabet No. 5, code defined in IT--T Recommendation T.50 (commonly known as “ASCII”).

notes.front: What does a parity bit add to an ASCII character?
notes.back: The ability to detect some types of errors.
notes.explanation: It only detects, and only some errors: it does not speed transmission, improve signal-to-noise ratio or enlarge the character set.
notes.example: Like a check digit on a card number, which shows a mistyped digit without saying which.
notes.evidence: What is the advantage of including parity bits in ASCII characters? A. Faster transmission rate B. Signal-to-noise ratio is improved C. A larger character set is available D. Some types of errors can be detected

notes.front: What does IMD stand for, and what does it evaluate in an AFSK signal?
notes.back: Intermodulation distortion: it evaluates distortion caused by excessive input audio levels.
notes.explanation: For an idling PSK signal, the pool's acceptable maximum IMD is −30 dB.
notes.example: Like the distortion from turning a computer's sound output up too far into the radio's audio input.
notes.evidence: What parameter evaluates distortion of an AFSK signal caused by excessive input audio levels? A. Signal-to-noise ratio B. Baud error rate C. Repeat Request Rate (RRR) D. Intermodulation Distortion (IMD)

notes.front: In an amateur mesh network, what is an IP address?
notes.back: An Internet Protocol address: the kind of address every node has.
notes.explanation: Nodes form the mesh by discovery and link establishment protocols, then reach each other by these addresses.
notes.example: Like a house number on a street, but for a radio node.
notes.evidence: E8C14 (C) What type of addresses do nodes have in a mesh network? A. Email B. Trust server C. Internet Protocol (IP) D. Talk group ~~ E8C15 (C) What technique do individual nodes use to form a mesh network? A. Forward error correction and Viterbi codes B. Acting as store-and-forward digipeaters C. Discovery and link establishment protocols

notes.front: How does direct sequence spread spectrum spread a signal?
notes.back: A high-speed binary bit stream shifts the phase of the RF carrier.
notes.explanation: It works on the carrier's phase, whereas frequency hopping moves the carrier's frequency.
notes.example: Like smearing a message across a wide band with a fast code that the right receiver can undo.
notes.evidence: E8D02 (B) What spread spectrum communications technique uses a high-speed binary bit stream to shift the phase of an RF carrier? A. Frequency hopping B. Direct sequence

notes.front: In frequency-hopping spread spectrum, what does the pseudorandom sequence decide?
notes.back: The order in which the transmitted frequency is varied.
notes.explanation: The hops follow the sequence, not what the receiver hears, so the pattern is set in advance.
notes.example: Like a shuffled playlist that looks random but can be played again in exactly the same order.
notes.evidence: D. Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence

notes.front: What is frequency hopping?
notes.back: Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence.
notes.explanation: It spreads the signal by moving its frequency, where direct sequence works on the carrier's phase.
notes.example: Like two people agreeing to change channel every second in a pre-arranged order.
notes.evidence: D. Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence

notes.front: What is fitted in a transmitter's keying system to prevent key clicks?
notes.back: A key-click filter.
notes.explanation: It sits in the keying system, where the sudden switching that produces the clicks and thumps happens.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 1, key clicks, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: interference may be present in the form of "clicks" or "thumps." KEY-CLICK FILTERS are used in the keying systems of radio transmitters to prevent such interference.

notes.front: Under Part 97, what must emissions outside the necessary bandwidth not cause?
notes.back: Splatter or key-click interference to operations on adjacent frequencies.
notes.explanation: The rule follows the requirement that emissions from modulation stay within the band or segment the control operator may use.
notes.evidence: Emissions resulting from modulation must be confined to the band or segment available to the control operator. Emissions outside the necessary bandwidth must not cause splatter or keyclick interference to operations on adjacent frequencies.

notes.front: How many code elements does the Baudot code use for each character?
notes.back: Five: it is the five-unit (five-level) teletypewriter code.
notes.explanation: The sending device divides each character's sending time into five short code elements of equal duration.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 3, teletypewriter codes, p. 3-17
notes.evidence: The FIVE-UNIT (five-level) CODE has been the most commonly used in modern printing telegraphy and is universally used in teletypewriter operation. This is also known as the Baudot code. The mechanical sending device in the teletypewriter divides the sending time for each character into five short code elements (impulses) of equal duration.

notes.front: What is Quadrature Amplitude Modulation or QAM?
notes.choices:
A) A technique for digital data compression used in digital television which removes redundancy in the data by comparing bit amplitudes
B) Transmission of data by modulating the amplitude of two carriers of the same frequency but 90 degrees out of phase
C) A method of performing single sideband modulation by shifting the phase of the carrier and modulation components of the signal
D) A technique for analog modulation of television video signals using phase modulation and compression
notes.back: Transmission of data by modulating the amplitude of two carriers of the same frequency but 90 degrees out of phase
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not a data-compression scheme. C: it is not a way of making single sideband. D: it is not an analog television modulation.
notes.explanation: The two carriers are in quadrature, and each is amplitude-modulated with data.
notes.evidence: What is Quadrature Amplitude Modulation or QAM?

notes.front: What is the definition of symbol rate in a digital transmission?
notes.choices:
A) The number of control characters in a message packet
B) The maximum rate at which the forward error correction code can make corrections
C) The rate at which the waveform changes to convey information
D) The number of characters carried per second by the station-to-station link
notes.back: The rate at which the waveform changes to convey information
notes.choicesExplained: A: control characters are content, not a signalling rate. B: error-correction capacity is not a symbol rate. D: characters per second is a text rate, not the symbol rate.
notes.explanation: Each change of the waveform carries information, so symbol rate counts those changes per second, the same as baud.
notes.evidence: What is the definition of symbol rate in a digital transmission?

notes.front: Why should the phase of a PSK signal be changed at the zero crossing of the RF signal?
notes.choices:
A) To minimize bandwidth
B) To simplify modulation
C) To improve carrier suppression
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: To minimize bandwidth
notes.choicesExplained: B: it does not simplify modulation. C: carrier suppression is not the reason. D: only bandwidth is the pool's answer.
notes.explanation: A phase change away from a zero crossing makes a sudden jump in voltage, which spreads energy across a wide band; at the zero crossing there is no jump.
notes.evidence: Why should the phase of a PSK signal be changed at the zero crossing of the RF signal?

notes.front: What technique minimizes the bandwidth of a PSK31 signal?
notes.choices:
A) Zero-sum character encoding
B) Reed-Solomon character encoding
C) Use of sinusoidal data pulses
D) Use of linear data pulses
notes.back: Use of sinusoidal data pulses
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: character encoding does not shape the pulses. D: linear data pulses are the distractor to sinusoidal ones.
notes.explanation: Smooth sinusoidal pulses have no sharp edges, and sharp edges are what spread a signal’s energy over a wide band.
notes.evidence: What technique minimizes the bandwidth of a PSK31 signal?

notes.front: What is the approximate bandwidth of a 13-WPM International Morse Code transmission?
notes.choices:
A) 13 Hz
B) 26 Hz
C) 52 Hz
D) 104 Hz
notes.back: 52 Hz
notes.choicesExplained: A: 13 Hz is just the speed figure. B: 26 Hz is only twice it. D: 104 Hz is double the pool's figure.
notes.explanation: A common rule of thumb puts CW bandwidth at about four times the speed in words per minute: 4 × 13 = 52 Hz.
notes.evidence: What is the approximate bandwidth of a 13-WPM International Morse Code transmission?

notes.front: What is the bandwidth of an FT8 signal?
notes.choices:
A) 10 Hz
B) 50 Hz
C) 600 Hz
D) 2.4 kHz
notes.back: 50 Hz
notes.choicesExplained: A: 10 Hz is too narrow. C: 600 Hz is twelve times too wide. D: 2.4 kHz is nearly fifty times too wide.
notes.explanation: FT8 sends one of 8 tones spaced 6.25 Hz apart, so the signal spans 8 × 6.25 = 50 Hz.
notes.evidence: What is the bandwidth of an FT8 signal?

notes.front: What is the bandwidth of a 4,800-Hz frequency shift, 9,600-baud ASCII FM transmission?
notes.choices:
A) 15.36 kHz
B) 9.6 kHz
C) 4.8 kHz
D) 5.76 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: B: 9.6 kHz is the baud term alone. C: 4.8 kHz is the shift alone. D: 5.76 kHz is only the 1.2 × shift term, without the baud rate.
notes.explanation: A common formula for FSK bandwidth is the baud rate plus 1.2 times the shift: 9,600 + (1.2 × 4,800) = 9,600 + 5,760 = 15,360 Hz, or 15.36 kHz.
notes.evidence: What is the bandwidth of a 4,800-Hz frequency shift, 9,600-baud ASCII FM transmission?

notes.front: How does ARQ accomplish error correction?
notes.choices:
A) Special binary codes provide automatic correction
B) Special polynomial codes provide automatic correction
C) If errors are detected, redundant data is substituted
D) If errors are detected, a retransmission is requested
notes.back: If errors are detected, a retransmission is requested
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: automatic correction by special codes describes forward error correction. C: substituting redundant data is not what ARQ does.
notes.explanation: ARQ detects errors and asks for the data again; correcting without asking is forward error correction.
notes.evidence: How does ARQ accomplish error correction?

notes.front: Which digital code allows only one bit to change between sequential code values?
notes.choices:
A) Binary Coded Decimal Code
B) Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
C) Extended ASCII
D) Gray code
notes.back: Gray code
notes.choicesExplained: A: binary coded decimal can change several bits at once, as from 7 to 8. B: that interchange code is a character code without the one-bit property. C: extended ASCII is a character set, not a one-bit-change code.
notes.explanation: Gray code is arranged so that each step to the next value flips exactly one bit.
notes.evidence: Which digital code allows only one bit to change between sequential code values?

notes.front: How can data rate be increased without increasing bandwidth?
notes.choices:
A) It is impossible
B) Increasing analog-to-digital conversion resolution
C) Using a more efficient digital code
D) Using forward error correction
notes.back: Using a more efficient digital code
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is possible, by coding. B: converter resolution concerns digitising, not the data rate on air. D: forward error correction is for correcting errors, not for raising the data rate.
notes.explanation: A more efficient code carries more bits in each symbol, for example by using more phase or amplitude states, so data rate rises while the symbol rate, and so the bandwidth, stays the same.
notes.evidence: How can data rate be increased without increasing bandwidth?

notes.front: What is the relationship between symbol rate and baud?
notes.choices:
A) They are the same
B) Baud is twice the symbol rate
C) Baud rate is half the symbol rate
D) The relationship depends on the specific code used
notes.back: They are the same
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: neither is twice or half the other. D: the relationship does not depend on the code.
notes.explanation: Both count how many times per second the waveform changes to convey information.
notes.evidence: What is the relationship between symbol rate and baud?

notes.front: What factors affect the bandwidth of a transmitted CW signal?
notes.choices:
A) IF bandwidth and Q
B) Modulation index and output power
C) Keying speed and shape factor (rise and fall time)
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: Keying speed and shape factor (rise and fall time)
notes.choicesExplained: A: IF bandwidth and Q are receiver properties. B: modulation index is an FM measure, and output power is not the pool's answer. D: only C is correct.
notes.explanation: Keying speed and the keying waveform's shape set the width; very short rise and fall times also cause key clicks.
notes.evidence: What factors affect the bandwidth of a transmitted CW signal?

notes.front: What is described by the constellation diagram of a QAM or QPSK signal?
notes.choices:
A) How many carriers may be present at the same time
B) The possible phase and amplitude states for each symbol
C) Frequency response of the signal stream
D) The number of bits used for error correction in the protocol
notes.back: The possible phase and amplitude states for each symbol
notes.choicesExplained: A: it does not count carriers. C: frequency response is a different kind of plot. D: error-correction bits are not shown.
notes.explanation: Each point on the diagram is one possible phase-and-amplitude state for a symbol.
notes.evidence: What is described by the constellation diagram of a QAM or QPSK signal?

notes.front: What type of addresses do nodes have in a mesh network?
notes.choices:
A) Email
B) Trust server
C) Internet Protocol (IP)
D) Talk group
notes.back: Internet Protocol (IP)
notes.choicesExplained: A: email addresses belong to users, not nodes. B: 'trust server' is a distractor. D: talk groups belong to DMR.
notes.explanation: Mesh nodes are addressed like computers on the internet, with Internet Protocol addresses.
notes.evidence: What type of addresses do nodes have in a mesh network?

notes.front: What technique do individual nodes use to form a mesh network?
notes.choices:
A) Forward error correction and Viterbi codes
B) Acting as store-and-forward digipeaters
C) Discovery and link establishment protocols
D) Custom code plugs for the local trunking systems
notes.back: Discovery and link establishment protocols
notes.choicesExplained: A: error-correcting codes do not build a network. B: store-and-forward digipeating belongs to packet radio. D: code plugs configure trunked or DMR radios.
notes.explanation: Each node discovers its neighbours and establishes links with them, forming the mesh.
notes.evidence: What technique do individual nodes use to form a mesh network?

notes.front: Why are received spread spectrum signals resistant to interference?
notes.choices:
A) Signals not using the spread spectrum algorithm are suppressed in the receiver
B) The high power used by a spread spectrum transmitter keeps its signal from being easily overpowered
C) Built-in error correction codes minimize interference
D) If the receiver detects interference, it will signal the transmitter to change frequencies
notes.back: Signals not using the spread spectrum algorithm are suppressed in the receiver
notes.choicesExplained: B: spread spectrum does not rely on high power. C: error-correction codes are not the reason. D: a receiver asking for a frequency change is not how spread spectrum works.
notes.explanation: The receiver de-spreads with the same code: the wanted signal collapses back to a narrow band, while any other signal is spread out and mostly filtered away.
notes.evidence: Why are received spread spectrum signals resistant to interference?

notes.front: What spread spectrum communications technique uses a high-speed binary bit stream to shift the phase of an RF carrier?
notes.choices:
A) Frequency hopping
B) Direct sequence
C) Binary phase-shift keying
D) Phase compandored spread spectrum
notes.back: Direct sequence
notes.choicesExplained: A: frequency hopping changes frequency, not phase. C: BPSK on its own is not spread spectrum. D: 'phase compandored' is a distractor.
notes.explanation: The fast bit stream shifts the carrier's phase and so spreads it: that is direct sequence.
notes.evidence: What spread spectrum communications technique uses a high-speed binary bit stream to shift the phase of an RF carrier?

notes.front: Which describes spread spectrum frequency hopping?
notes.choices:
A) If interference is detected by the receiver, it will signal the transmitter to change frequencies
B) RF signals are clipped to generate a wide band of harmonics which provides redundancy to correct errors
C) A binary bit stream is used to shift the phase of an RF carrier very rapidly in a pseudorandom sequence
D) Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence
notes.back: Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence
notes.choicesExplained: A: hopping does not wait for the receiver to report interference. B: clipping to make harmonics is not spread spectrum. C: phase shifts from a bit stream describe direct sequence.
notes.explanation: The hops follow a pseudorandom sequence, not reports of interference.
notes.evidence: Which describes spread spectrum frequency hopping?

notes.front: What is the primary effect of extremely short rise or fall time on a CW signal?
notes.choices:
A) More difficult to copy
B) The generation of RF harmonics
C) The generation of key clicks
D) More difficult to tune
notes.back: The generation of key clicks
notes.choicesExplained: A: copying difficulty is not the main effect. B: harmonics are not the pool's answer. D: tuning is not affected.
notes.explanation: Very short rise or fall times mean sudden application and removal of power, which causes clicks heard far from the transmitter's frequency.
notes.evidence: What is the primary effect of extremely short rise or fall time on a CW signal?

notes.front: What is the most common method of reducing key clicks?
notes.choices:
A) Increase keying waveform rise and fall times
B) Insert low-pass filters at the transmitter output
C) Reduce keying waveform rise and fall times
D) Insert high-pass filters at the transmitter output
notes.back: Increase keying waveform rise and fall times
notes.choicesExplained: B: a low-pass output filter is not the common cure. C: shorter rise and fall times cause key clicks. D: a high-pass filter does nothing about the keying.
notes.explanation: Slower edges make the keying less sudden, and it is sudden application and removal of power that causes clicks.
notes.evidence: What is the most common method of reducing key clicks?

notes.front: What is the advantage of including parity bits in ASCII characters?
notes.choices:
A) Faster transmission rate
B) Signal-to-noise ratio is improved
C) A larger character set is available
D) Some types of errors can be detected
notes.back: Some types of errors can be detected
notes.choicesExplained: A: it adds a bit, so it does not speed transmission. B: it does not improve signal-to-noise ratio. C: it does not enlarge the character set.
notes.explanation: A parity bit lets the receiver detect some types of error, though not all of them.
notes.evidence: What is the advantage of including parity bits in ASCII characters?

notes.front: What is a common cause of overmodulation of AFSK signals?
notes.choices:
A) Excessive numbers of retries
B) Excessive frequency deviation
C) Bit errors in the modem
D) Excessive transmit audio levels
notes.back: Excessive transmit audio levels
notes.choicesExplained: A: retries follow poor copy; they do not overmodulate. B: excessive deviation is not the pool's answer for AFSK. C: modem bit errors do not overmodulate the transmitter.
notes.explanation: Excessive transmit audio is the common cause; IMD is the measure used to spot the resulting distortion.
notes.evidence: What is a common cause of overmodulation of AFSK signals?

notes.front: What parameter evaluates distortion of an AFSK signal caused by excessive input audio levels?
notes.choices:
A) Signal-to-noise ratio
B) Baud error rate
C) Repeat Request Rate (RRR)
D) Intermodulation Distortion (IMD)
notes.back: Intermodulation Distortion (IMD)
notes.choicesExplained: A: signal-to-noise ratio measures noise, not overdrive distortion. B and C: 'baud error rate' and 'repeat request rate' are distractors.
notes.explanation: The pool names IMD as the parameter for judging distortion from excessive input audio; for idling PSK its acceptable maximum is −30 dB.
notes.evidence: What parameter evaluates distortion of an AFSK signal caused by excessive input audio levels?

notes.front: What is considered an acceptable maximum IMD level for an idling PSK signal?
notes.choices:
A) +5 dB
B) +10 dB
C) +15 dB
D) -30 dB
notes.back: -30 dB
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: positive IMD figures are all far above the −30 dB maximum.
notes.explanation: The pool's acceptable maximum for an idling PSK signal is −30 dB; each positive figure is far above it.
notes.evidence: What is considered an acceptable maximum IMD level for an idling PSK signal?

notes.front: What are some of the differences between the Baudot digital code and ASCII?
notes.choices:
A) Baudot uses 4 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot uses 1 character as a letters/figures shift code, ASCII has no letters/figures code
B) Baudot uses 5 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot uses 2 characters as letters/figures shift codes, ASCII has no letters/figures shift code
C) Baudot uses 6 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot has no letters/figures shift code, ASCII uses 2 letters/figures shift codes
D) Baudot uses 7 data bits per character, ASCII uses 8; Baudot has no letters/figures shift code, ASCII uses 2 letters/figures shift codes
notes.back: Baudot uses 5 data bits and 2 letters/figures shift codes; ASCII uses 7 or 8 bits and has no letters/figures shift code.
notes.choicesExplained: A: Baudot uses 5 data bits, not 4. C and D: it is Baudot that has letters/figures shift codes, not ASCII.
notes.explanation: Baudot is the 5-unit teletypewriter code; Part 97 lists ASCII as a 7-unit code.
notes.evidence: What are some of the differences between the Baudot digital code and ASCII?

notes.front: What is one advantage of using ASCII code for data communications?
notes.choices:
A) It includes built-in error correction features
B) It contains fewer information bits per character than any other code
C) It is possible to transmit both uppercase and lowercase text
D) It uses one character as a shift code to send numeric and special characters
notes.back: It is possible to transmit both uppercase and lowercase text
notes.choicesExplained: A: ASCII has no built-in error correction; parity bits only detect some errors. B: it has more bits per character than Baudot, not fewer. D: using a shift code describes Baudot.
notes.explanation: ASCII can carry both upper and lower case text, where Baudot relies on letters/figures shifts.
notes.evidence: What is one advantage of using ASCII code for data communications?

notes.front: The pool puts Morse at 13 words per minute about 52 Hz wide. On the same basis, about how wide is CW sent at 25 words per minute?
notes.choices:
A) 25 Hz
B) 50 Hz
C) 100 Hz
D) 400 Hz
notes.back: 100 Hz
notes.choicesExplained: A: 25 Hz is just the speed figure. B: 50 Hz is the width at about half this speed. D: 400 Hz is four times too wide.
notes.explanation: Keying speed sets CW bandwidth, and 52 Hz at 13 words per minute is 4 Hz per word per minute: 4 × 25 = 100 Hz.
notes.evidence: E8C05 (C) What is the approximate bandwidth of a 13-WPM International Morse Code transmission? A. 13 Hz B. 26 Hz C. 52 Hz

notes.front: Which of these 2-bit counting sequences is a Gray code?
notes.choicesExplained: A: going from 01 to 10 changes both bits. C: going from 00 to 11 changes both bits. D: every step changes both bits.
notes.explanation: In a Gray code only one bit changes between sequential values, and only sequence B keeps to that at every step.
notes.evidence: Which digital code allows only one bit to change between sequential code values?

notes.front: A club's ASCII data link needs a way for the receiver to detect some errors, without changing the character set. What should be added?
notes.choices:
A) A parity bit on each character
B) A switch to Baudot
C) More transmitter power
D) Gray-coded characters
notes.back: A parity bit on each character
notes.choicesExplained: B: Baudot is a different, 5-bit code, not an error check. C: power adds no error checking. D: Gray code limits bit changes between sequential values; it is not an error check.
notes.explanation: Including parity bits in ASCII characters lets some types of errors be detected.
notes.evidence: What is the advantage of including parity bits in ASCII characters? A. Faster transmission rate B. Signal-to-noise ratio is improved C. A larger character set is available D. Some types of errors can be detected

notes.front: A data link's receiver finds an error in a block and sends a request for that block again. Which error-control scheme is this?
notes.choices:
A) ARQ
B) Forward error correction
C) Gray coding
D) Dither
notes.back: ARQ
notes.choicesExplained: B: forward error correction corrects without asking for a retransmission. C: Gray code is a counting code, not error control. D: dither is noise added to an ADC's input.
notes.explanation: ARQ accomplishes error correction by requesting a retransmission whenever errors are detected.
notes.evidence: E8C08 (D) How does ARQ accomplish error correction? A. Special binary codes provide automatic correction B. Special polynomial codes provide automatic correction C. If errors are detected, redundant data is substituted D. If errors are detected, a retransmission is requested

notes.front: Stations well away from your frequency report clicks whenever you send CW. What change to the keying waveform is the usual cure?
notes.choices:
A) Lengthen its rise and fall times
B) Shorten its rise and fall times
C) Raise the keying speed
D) Fit a high-pass filter at the output
notes.back: Lengthen its rise and fall times
notes.choicesExplained: B: shorter rise and fall times cause key clicks. C: faster keying widens a CW signal rather than curing clicks. D: a high-pass filter does nothing about the keying.
notes.explanation: Increasing the keying waveform's rise and fall times is the most common way of reducing key clicks.
notes.evidence: E8D05 (A) What is the most common method of reducing key clicks? A. Increase keying waveform rise and fall times

notes.front: An AFSK data signal is overmodulated and its IMD is poor. What is the most likely cause to correct first?
notes.choices:
A) Excessive transmit audio level
B) Too many retries
C) Bit errors in the modem
D) Too little transmitter power
notes.back: Excessive transmit audio level
notes.choicesExplained: B: retries follow poor copy; they do not overmodulate. C: modem bit errors do not overmodulate the transmitter. D: low power does not cause overmodulation.
notes.explanation: Excessive transmit audio is the common cause of AFSK overmodulation, and IMD is how that distortion is judged.
notes.evidence: E8D07 (D) What is a common cause of overmodulation of AFSK signals? A. Excessive numbers of retries B. Excessive frequency deviation C. Bit errors in the modem D. Excessive transmit audio levels

notes.front: Two stations idling on PSK measure their IMD: one reads −35 dB, the other −22 dB. Which is within the acceptable maximum?
notes.choices:
A) Only the −35 dB station
B) Only the −22 dB station
C) Both
D) Neither
notes.back: Only the −35 dB station
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: −22 dB is above the −30 dB maximum. D: −35 dB is below the maximum, so it is acceptable.
notes.explanation: The acceptable maximum IMD for an idling PSK signal is −30 dB; −35 dB is under it and −22 dB is over it.
notes.evidence: E8D09 (D) What is considered an acceptable maximum IMD level for an idling PSK signal? A. +5 dB B. +10 dB C. +15 dB D. -30 dB

notes.front: A monitoring receiver shows a signal jumping rapidly from frequency to frequency in a pattern that looks random but repeats. Which spread spectrum technique is it?
notes.choices:
A) Frequency hopping
B) Direct sequence
C) Quadrature amplitude modulation
D) Time division multiplexing
notes.back: Frequency hopping
notes.choicesExplained: B: direct sequence shifts the carrier's phase with a fast bit stream rather than moving its frequency. C: QAM is not spread spectrum. D: TDM shares time slots; it does not hop.
notes.explanation: Frequency hopping rapidly varies the transmitted frequency according to a pseudorandom sequence.
notes.evidence: D. Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence

notes.front: A modem changes its waveform 300 times a second to convey data. What are its symbol rate and its baud?
notes.choices:
A) 300 symbols per second and 300 baud
B) 300 symbols per second and 600 baud
C) 150 symbols per second and 300 baud
D) It depends on the code used
notes.back: 300 symbols per second and 300 baud
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: baud is neither twice nor half the symbol rate. D: the two are the same whatever the code.
notes.explanation: Symbol rate is the rate at which the waveform changes to convey information, and symbol rate and baud are the same.
notes.evidence: E8C11 (A) What is the relationship between symbol rate and baud? A. They are the same

notes.front: You need to send a message in mixed upper and lower case text. Which code allows it: Baudot or ASCII?
notes.choices:
A) ASCII
B) Baudot
C) Either
D) Neither
notes.back: ASCII
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: Baudot uses letters/figures shift characters, and the pool credits only ASCII with both cases. D: ASCII allows it.
notes.explanation: One advantage of ASCII for data communications is that both uppercase and lowercase text can be sent.
notes.evidence: E8D11 (C) What is one advantage of using ASCII code for data communications? A. It includes built-in error correction features B. It contains fewer information bits per character than any other code C. It is possible to transmit both uppercase and lowercase text

notes.front: How does direct sequence spread spectrum differ from frequency hopping?
notes.back: Direct sequence shifts the carrier's phase with a high-speed bit stream; frequency hopping varies the carrier's frequency in a pseudorandom sequence.
notes.explanation: Both spread the signal; they differ in whether the carrier's phase or its frequency is changed.
notes.evidence: E8D02 (B) What spread spectrum communications technique uses a high-speed binary bit stream to shift the phase of an RF carrier? A. Frequency hopping B. Direct sequence

notes.front: How do the Baudot code and ASCII differ in bits and shift codes?
notes.back: Baudot: 5 data bits, with two letters/figures shift characters. ASCII: 7 or 8 data bits, and no shift code.
notes.explanation: The pool also credits ASCII with being able to send both upper and lower case text.
notes.evidence: B. Baudot uses 5 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot uses 2 characters as letters/figures shift codes, ASCII has no letters/figures shift code
